data.name: Angular SPA
data.description: Client-side Angular 21.x single-page application serving the Juice Shop storefront, challenge UI, and admin views. Executes in the user's browser; communicates with the Express backend over REST and Socket.IO, storing JWT tokens in localStorage.

threats.title: [F-006] Predictable derived password (frontend/src/app/oauth/oauth.component.ts:30)
threats.description:
An attacker who knows any OAuth user's e-mail address computes that user's shop password offline as btoa(email reversed), because OAuthComponent registers and logs in the account with exactly that value; the attacker then authenticates through the ordinary /rest/user/login form without touching Google at all.

Impact: Every account created through the Google login path is takeable by anyone who learns the e-mail address, giving access to that user's basket, order history, addresses, and stored payment methods, and to the admin panel if an administrator ever signed in through OAuth.

Risk: Critical (likelihood High, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-522
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
oauth.component.ts:30 sets `const password = btoa(profile.email.split('').reverse().join(''))` and passes it to userService.save(), and line 46 reuses the identical expression to log in, so the credential is a pure function of the public identity claim.
- frontend/src/app/oauth/oauth.component.ts:30

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-006 (F-006)
threats.mitigation:
M-006 — Use OAuth authorization code flow with PKCE (priority P1, effort Medium)
1. Remove the btoa(reversed email) password derivation at frontend/src/app/oauth/oauth.component.ts:30 and :46 and let the server establish the federated session from the verified token alone, with no local password created for the account.
2. Where a local credential must exist for legacy reasons, have the server generate it with a CSPRNG and never return or reconstruct it in the browser.
3. Add a spec asserting that OAuthComponent issues no userService.save() call carrying a password field.
Verification: Run `npx vitest run frontend/src/app/oauth/oauth.component.spec.ts`; assert that the request body captured for /api/Users contains no `password` property and that login is driven by the OAuth token only.
Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/522.html

threats.title: [F-009] Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
threats.description: An attacker sends a victim a link such as /#/search?q=, and filterTable() passes the raw query parameter through DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml into the searchValue binding, which the template renders with [innerHTML]; the payload executes in the shop origin with no Content-Security-Policy to stop it and reads the JWT the SPA keeps in localStorage. Impact: Any user who opens an attacker-crafted search link loses their session JWT and can have arbitrary requests issued as themselves; if the victim is an administrator the same payload reaches the admin panel and its user and feedback management actions. Risk: Critical (likelihood High, impact Critical) CWE: CWE-79 Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable Source: stride Evidence: search-result.component.ts:136-143 reads route.snapshot.queryParams.q and assigns this.searchValue = sanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml(queryParam); search-result.component.html:11 binds that value with [innerHTML], completing an unescaped source-to-sink path from the URL. - frontend/src/app/search-result/search-result.component.ts:143 Abuse-case trace: - AC-T-001 [partially blocked, verification complete] — Account Takeover via Stored XSS + Token Hijacking; matching steps 1 (confirmed) Full finding: threat-model.md#f-009 (F-009)
threats.mitigation: M-009 — Encode output instead of bypassing the framework sanitizer (priority P1, effort Low) 1. Remove the bypassSecurityTrustHtml call at frontend/src/app/search-result/search-result.component.ts:143 and keep searchValue a plain string. 2. Change frontend/src/app/search-result/search-result.component.html:11 from [innerHTML]="searchValue" to an interpolated {{ searchValue }} binding so Angular escapes the value. 3. Replace the assertion in search-result.component.spec.ts that currently expects bypassSecurityTrustHtml to be called with '' by one asserting the rendered #searchValue element contains the payload as text and no script node. Verification: Run `npx vitest run frontend/src/app/search-result/search-result.component.spec.ts`; loading q= must leave querySelector('#searchValue img') null and the escaped text present. Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/79.html

threats.title: [F-015] Implicit OAuth flow (frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:148)
threats.description:
An attacker lures a victim to a page that redirects to the shop's own OAuth entry point, or replays a fragment of their choosing, because googleLogin() starts a bare implicit flow with response_type=token and sends no state, nonce, or PKCE challenge; the route matcher then accepts any URL carrying '#access_token=' (frontend/src/app/app.routing.ts:286) and OAuthComponent parses the fragment by string splitting and posts the token straight to /rest/user/oauth without checking that this browser started the flow.

Impact: A victim can be silently logged into an account the attacker controls (session fixation on the shop), or an attacker-obtained Google access token can be injected into the victim's browser to bind their shop session to a foreign identity; orders, addresses, and payment data are then created under the wrong account.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-287
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
login.component.ts:148 builds the authorization URL with response_type=token and only client_id, scope, and redirect_uri; no state or nonce parameter is generated or stored, and oauth.component.ts:70-79 parses the returned fragment without comparing any request-binding value.
- frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:148

Abuse-case trace:
- AC-T-001 [partially blocked, verification complete] — Account Takeover via Stored XSS + Token Hijacking; matching steps 3 (confirmed)

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-015 (F-015)
threats.mitigation:
M-015 — Harden the authentication flow (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Change googleLogin() in frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:148 to request response_type=code with code_challenge_method=S256, a CSPRNG-generated code_verifier, and a CSPRNG-generated state and nonce held in sessionStorage.
2. Reject the callback in frontend/src/app/oauth/oauth.component.ts unless the returned state exactly matches the stored value, and exchange the code server-side instead of parsing an access token out of window.location fragment.
3. Add a component test that drives OAuthComponent with a fragment carrying a mismatched state and asserts no call to userService.oauthLogin is made.
Verification: Run `npx vitest run frontend/src/app/oauth/oauth.component.spec.ts` with the new negative case; a callback whose state does not match the stored value must leave isLoggedIn false and issue no /rest/user/oauth request.
Reference: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9700#name-implicit-grant

threats.title: [F-030] Session token in localStorage (frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:101)
threats.description:
An attacker who achieves script execution through any of this component's HTML-injection sinks, or who has possession of the device, reads the session JWT directly with localStorage.getItem('token'), because the SPA persists the token in localStorage on every login path and re-reads it from there for routing and API calls.

Impact: One successful injection or one moment of device access hands over a full session token that authenticates every subsequent API call, including administrative ones when the victim holds the admin role.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-922
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
login.component.ts:101 stores the authentication token in localStorage; the same write occurs at oauth.component.ts:51 and two-factor-auth-enter.component.ts:53, and request.interceptor.ts:13 and app.guard.ts:18 read it back, so no HttpOnly boundary ever protects it.
- frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:101

Abuse-case trace:
- AC-T-001 [partially blocked, verification complete] — Account Takeover via Stored XSS + Token Hijacking; matching steps 2 (confirmed)

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-030 (F-030)
threats.mitigation:
M-030 — Store session tokens in HttpOnly, Secure cookies (priority P2, effort High)
1. Have the API set the session token as an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict cookie at login and delete the localStorage writes at frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:101, frontend/src/app/oauth/oauth.component.ts:51, and frontend/src/app/two-factor-auth-enter/two-factor-auth-enter.component.ts:53.
2. Drop the Authorization header logic in frontend/src/app/Services/request.interceptor.ts:13-19 in favour of withCredentials, and add CSRF protection for state-changing calls now authenticated by an ambient cookie.
3. Add specs asserting that no login path writes a token to localStorage and that state-changing requests carry the CSRF token.
Verification: Run `npx vitest run frontend/src/app/login/login.component.spec.ts frontend/src/app/Services/request.interceptor.spec.ts`; after a successful login localStorage.getItem('token') must be null and requests must be issued with withCredentials true.
Reference: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/HTML5_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html#local-storage

threats.title: [F-040] Client-side-only authorization guard (frontend/src/app/app.guard.ts:54)
threats.description:
An attacker edits the localStorage 'token' entry to a JWT whose payload claims data.role = 'admin', and AdminGuard admits the route because tokenDecode() uses jwtDecode, which reads the payload without verifying the signature; the administration and accounting views and their privileged API-calling code then load in the attacker's browser.

Impact: Any user can render the administration and accounting interfaces and trigger their privileged requests, so protection of user records, feedback deletion, and order data rests entirely on server-side checks the SPA neither performs nor verifies.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-602
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
app.guard.ts:35-38 reads the token from localStorage and decodes it with jwtDecode (a decode-only helper, no key or verification), and lines 54, 70, and 86 make the admin, accounting, and deluxe decisions solely from that unverified payload; app.routing.ts:81 attaches AdminGuard as the only protection on the /administration route.
- frontend/src/app/app.guard.ts:54

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-040 (F-040)
threats.mitigation:
M-040 — Enforce authorization on the server (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Change AdminGuard and AccountingGuard in frontend/src/app/app.guard.ts:52-76 to resolve the route from a server response (for example an authenticated /rest/user/whoami role lookup) instead of a locally decoded JWT payload.
2. Confirm every administrative API the panel calls enforces the role server-side, and treat the guard purely as a navigation convenience.
3. Add a guard spec that plants a self-made token whose payload claims the admin role and asserts canActivate resolves false when the server reports a non-admin role.
Verification: Run `npx vitest run frontend/src/app/app.guard.spec.ts` with a forged unsigned token claiming data.role='admin'; AdminGuard.canActivate must resolve false and navigate to /403.
Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/602.html

threats.title: [F-045] Missing Content Security Policy (frontend/src/index.html:9)
threats.description:
An attacker exploiting any of the confirmed HTML-injection sinks faces no script-source restriction, because the SPA shell declares no Content-Security-Policy: a grep of frontend/src for a CSP or any http-equiv meta directive returns zero hits, so injected inline handlers and external script loads both execute, and the page can also be framed for clickjacking.

Impact: Every injection finding in this component escalates from limited HTML to full script execution with external exfiltration, and no frame-ancestors directive limits embedding of the storefront in an attacker page.

Risk: Medium (likelihood High, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-693
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
frontend/src/index.html:9-16 declares only charset, description, viewport, preconnect and favicon meta/link tags; a zero-hit search for 'content-security-policy|http-equiv' across frontend/src proves no policy is declared in the delivered document.
- frontend/src/index.html:9

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-045 (F-045)
threats.mitigation:
M-045 — Declare a script-src and frame-ancestors policy for the SPA shell (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Serve a Content-Security-Policy response header for frontend/src/index.html with script-src 'self' plus per-response nonces, object-src 'none', base-uri 'self', and frame-ancestors 'none', and drop 'unsafe-inline' by moving the inline cookie-consent script at frontend/src/index.html:17 into a bundled file.
2. Roll the policy out in report-only mode first, collect violation reports, then enforce.
3. Add a build or end-to-end assertion that the served document carries the enforcing header.
Verification: curl -sI http://localhost:3000/ | grep -i content-security-policy must return an enforcing policy containing script-src and frame-ancestors, and the app must load with no console CSP violations.
Reference: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Content_Security_Policy_Cheat_Sheet.html

threats.title: [F-047] Forgeable identity header (frontend/src/app/Services/request.interceptor.ts:23)
threats.description:
A user opens developer tools, rewrites the localStorage 'email' entry to another person's address, and every subsequent API call carries X-User-Email with that forged value, because the interceptor copies browser-writable storage into an identity header on all outgoing requests; any server-side record or decision keyed on that header then names the wrong account.

Impact: Actions logged or attributed by X-User-Email cannot be tied back to the account that actually performed them, so a user can repudiate purchases, complaints, or data changes and investigators cannot reconstruct who acted.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-290
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
request.interceptor.ts:20-25 reads localStorage.getItem('email') and sets it as the X-User-Email header on every request, and login.component.ts:135 shows that value is written from the user's own form input, never from a server-verified source.
- frontend/src/app/Services/request.interceptor.ts:23

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-047 (F-047)
threats.mitigation:
M-047 — Stop sending a client-asserted identity header from request.interceptor.ts (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Remove the X-User-Email header block at frontend/src/app/Services/request.interceptor.ts:20-26 so the JWT remains the only identity the SPA transmits.
2. Where a display e-mail is needed by an endpoint, have the server resolve it from the verified token subject instead of the request header.
3. Add an interceptor spec asserting no X-User-Email header is present on outgoing requests even when localStorage holds an 'email' entry.
Verification: Run `npx vitest run frontend/src/app/Services/request.interceptor.spec.ts`; with localStorage.email set, the captured HttpRequest must carry Authorization only and no X-User-Email header.
Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/290.html

threats.title: [F-060] Hardcoded test credentials (frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:62)
threats.description:
An attacker opens the shipped JavaScript bundle, reads the literal account name and password compiled into LoginComponent, and submits them to /rest/user/login to obtain a session without any guessing.

Impact: Anyone who views the bundle obtains a working credential pair for the shop, giving whatever access that account holds without touching authentication controls such as rate limiting or lockout.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-798
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
login.component.ts:61-62 declares public testingUsername = 'testing@juice-sh.op' and public testingPassword = 'IamU**** (17 chars)' as component fields, so both literals are compiled into the client bundle delivered to every visitor.
- frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:62

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-060 (F-060)
threats.mitigation:
M-060 — Move secrets to a managed secret store (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Delete the testingUsername and testingPassword fields at frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:61-62; keep any test-only credential in the test fixtures that need it, not in shipped component code.
2. Rotate or disable the testing@juice-sh.op account server-side, since the password has been distributed in every build.
3. Add a CI grep over frontend/src that fails the build when a password-like literal is assigned to a component field.
Verification: Run `grep -rn "IamU**** (17 chars)" frontend/src` and require zero hits, and confirm the built bundle under frontend/dist contains no match.
Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/798.html

threats.title: [F-061] Session cookie without flags (frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:104)
threats.description:
An attacker reads or replays the duplicate session cookie the SPA writes itself, because cookieService.put('token', ...) is called from JavaScript with only an expiry, so the cookie is by construction not HttpOnly and carries neither Secure nor SameSite, leaving it readable by injected script and attachable to cross-site requests.

Impact: The session token exists in a second location that script can read and that the browser attaches to cross-site requests, widening both theft and cross-site request forgery exposure for authenticated actions.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-1004
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
login.component.ts:102-104 creates an eight-hour expiry and calls this.cookieService.put('token', authentication.token, { expires }) with no secure, httpOnly, or sameSite option; oauth.component.ts:50 repeats the same write.
- frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:104

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-061 (F-061)
threats.mitigation:
M-061 — Set secure session-cookie attributes (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Remove the client-side cookie writes at frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:104 and frontend/src/app/oauth/oauth.component.ts:50 and let the API issue the session cookie with HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite=Strict.
2. Keep the client-side removal path only for logout, or replace it with a server-side session invalidation call.
3. Add a spec asserting no document.cookie entry named token is created by the login flow.
Verification: Run `npx vitest run frontend/src/app/login/login.component.spec.ts` and assert document.cookie contains no token entry after login; in a browser, the token cookie must show HttpOnly and Secure in devtools.
Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1004.html

data.name: Express.js API Server
data.description: Node.js Express server hosting all REST API routes, Socket.IO real-time event handlers, and the AI chatbot endpoint backed by Ollama or OpenAI-compatible LLM providers. Runs on port 3000 and serves the compiled Angular frontend assets; includes LLM integration in routes/chat.ts co-deployed on the same listener.

threats.title: [F-001] JWT Verification Without Algorithm Allowlist
threats.description:
An anonymous internet attacker forges a JWT for any account because neither JWT verification path constrains the accepted algorithm. `updateAuthenticatedUsers` calls `jwt.verify(token, publicKey, cb)` at lib/insecurity.ts:189 with no `algorithms` option, and `isAuthorized()` at lib/insecurity.ts:52 builds `expressJwt({ secret: publicKey })` the same way. The verification key is the RS256 public key loaded from `encryptionkeys/jwt.pub` at lib/insecurity.ts:20, which ships in the repository, so the attacker signs an HS256 token using that public key text as the HMAC secret and both verifiers accept it.

Impact: Complete authentication bypass for every REST route on port 3000, including admin-only functions, order data, wallets, and payment methods.

Risk: Critical (likelihood High, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-347
CVSS v4: 9.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
lib/insecurity.ts:189 calls jwt.verify with only a key and a callback; no algorithms allowlist is passed, and the key at line 20 is an asymmetric public key.
- lib/insecurity.ts:189

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-1 external → api-server (internet-facing): The boundary assumes expressJwt proves caller identity, but the verifier accepts an attacker-chosen algorithm, so the authentication leg does not hold.

Abuse-case trace:
- AC-T-003 [fully viable, verification complete] — Privilege Escalation to Admin via JWT Algorithm Confusion; matching steps 1 (confirmed)
- AC-T-005 [fully viable, verification complete] — Authentication Bypass via Exposed Secret Material; matching steps 2 (confirmed)

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-001 (F-001)
threats.mitigation:
M-001 — Enforce JWT signature and algorithm verification (priority P1, effort Low)
1. Pass `algorithms: ['RS256']` to the jwt.verify call at lib/insecurity.ts:189 and to the expressJwt configuration at lib/insecurity.ts:52 so a token header can never select the accepted algorithm.
2. Add a negative test that signs a token HS256 with the contents of encryptionkeys/jwt.pub as the secret and asserts that a protected route returns 401.
Verification: Run the new test: `npm test -- --grep 'HS256 confusion'`; the request carrying the HS256-forged admin token must return HTTP 401 and no user context.
Reference: CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature

threats.title: [F-002] Missing Authentication on State-Changing Routes
threats.description:
An anonymous attacker reaches the archive and markup parsers because server.ts:309 registers `POST /file-upload` with only multer and the parsing chain `handleZipFileUpload, handleXmlUpload, handleYamlUpload`, and the authorization block that installs `security.updateAuthenticatedUsers()` and the route guards does not begin until server.ts:354. The image endpoints at server.ts:310 and server.ts:311 are registered in the same unguarded window; only `/rest/memories` at server.ts:312 carries `security.appendUserId()`. Registration order therefore places three attacker-reachable parsers outside the authentication boundary entirely.

Impact: Anonymous callers feed arbitrary archives and markup into server-side parsers and write into the publicly served uploads directory, without ever presenting a credential.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-862
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
server.ts:309 registers the file-upload route and its zip, XML, and YAML handlers with no security middleware, 45 lines before the authorization block starts at server.ts:354.
- server.ts:309

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-1 external → api-server (internet-facing): The authentication leg assumes every state-changing route is registered behind expressJwt, but three upload routes are registered before that middleware is installed.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-002 (F-002)
threats.mitigation:
M-002 — Enforce server-side authorization on every endpoint (priority P2, effort Low)
1. Relocate the registrations at server.ts:309-311 to after the authorization block that begins at server.ts:354, or add `security.isAuthorized()` as the first middleware on each of the three routes.
2. Add a test asserting anonymous POSTs to /file-upload, /profile/image/file, and /profile/image/url all return 401 before any parser runs.
Verification: POST a multipart body to /file-upload with no Authorization header and expect HTTP 401 with the zip handler spy showing zero invocations.
Reference: CWE-862: Missing Authorization

threats.title: [F-003] Missing Security Event Logging
threats.description:
An attacker who brute-forces or injects their way into an account leaves no attributable trace, because routes/login.ts:24 issues a session token without writing any security log entry, and the failure branch at routes/login.ts:50 returns 401 with no record either. A repository-wide search for audit-log identifiers across lib and routes returned zero hits, and neither routes/login.ts nor routes/resetPassword.ts imports the logger at all, so successful logins, failed logins, and password resets cannot be reconstructed after the fact.

Impact: Account takeover via the login SQL injection or JWT forgery cannot be detected, timed, or attributed during incident response.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-778
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
routes/login.ts:24 mints and stores a session token with no accompanying log call, and a zero-hit search confirms no audit-logging facility exists in lib or routes.
- routes/login.ts:24

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-003 (F-003)
threats.mitigation:
M-003 — Add security audit logging (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Log a structured event on both branches of routes/login.ts — success at line 24 and failure at line 50 — carrying timestamp, subject identifier, source address, and outcome, and never the submitted password.
2. Extend the same treatment to routes/resetPassword.ts and route the events to an append-only sink separate from the HTTP access log.
3. Add a test asserting that a failed login writes exactly one failure event containing no credential material.
Verification: Run the new test and assert the captured log stream contains one `auth.login.failure` record with the source address and no `password` key.
Reference: CWE-778: Insufficient Logging

threats.title: [F-004] Hardcoded RSA signing key in source (lib/insecurity.ts:21)
threats.description:
An attacker who can read the repository mints valid session tokens offline because the RSA private key used to sign every JWT is a string literal at lib/insecurity.ts:21. `authorize()` at lib/insecurity.ts:54 signs all authentication tokens with that constant, and `deluxeToken()` at lib/insecurity.ts:150 derives the deluxe membership HMAC from the same secret, so one disclosed literal defeats both session issuance and the deluxe entitlement check.

Impact: Offline forgery of any user or admin session and of deluxe entitlement tokens, with no server-side signal that the token was not issued by the application.

Risk: Critical (likelihood High, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-321
CVSS v4: 9.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: configuration-defect

Evidence:
lib/insecurity.ts:21 assigns a complete PEM-encoded RSA private key to a module constant that lib/insecurity.ts:54 uses as the JWT signing key.
- lib/insecurity.ts:21

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-1 external → api-server (internet-facing): The internet-facing boundary relies on JWT issuance to establish identity, but the signing key is a committed literal any reader can reuse to mint tokens.
- tb-2 external → auth-service (internet-facing): A token forged with the in-source private key satisfies the boundary without any password verification, breaking its authentication leg.

Abuse-case trace:
- AC-T-005 [fully viable, verification complete] — Authentication Bypass via Exposed Secret Material; matching steps 1 (confirmed)

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-004 (F-004)
threats.mitigation:
M-004 — Move cryptographic keys to a managed secret store (priority P1, effort Medium)
1. Replace the literal at lib/insecurity.ts:21 with a value read from an environment variable or secret store at startup, and fail startup when it is absent rather than falling back to a default.
2. Rotate the compromised key pair, regenerate encryptionkeys/jwt.pub, and add a startup test asserting the process exits non-zero when the signing key variable is unset.
Verification: Start the server with the signing-key variable unset and assert a non-zero exit; then grep the repository for `BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY` and expect zero hits outside test fixtures.
Reference: CWE-321: Use of Hard-coded Cryptographic Key

threats.title: [F-007] SQL Injection
threats.description:
An anonymous attacker authenticates as any account because routes/login.ts:34 builds the login query by interpolating `req.body.email` directly into `SELECT * FROM Users WHERE email = '...' AND password = '...'` and passes it to `models.sequelize.query`. No parameter binding or escaping is applied, so a quote plus comment sequence in the email field truncates the password predicate and the first returned row is handed to `afterLogin` at routes/login.ts:48, which issues a full session token.

Impact: Authentication bypass into arbitrary accounts including administrators, plus arbitrary read of the Users table through the same injection point.

Risk: Critical (likelihood High, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-89
CVSS v4: 9.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
routes/login.ts:34 concatenates req.body.email into a raw SQL string passed to sequelize.query, with no bind parameters.
- routes/login.ts:34

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-5 api-server → sqlite-database (internal): The SQLite boundary assumes every query reaches the database through Sequelize parameterization, but the login path emits a fully interpolated raw statement.

threats.title: [F-016] Prompt injection via unvalidated messages (routes/chat.ts:191)
threats.description:
LLM01 — Prompt Injection: an anonymous caller overrides the chatbot's behavioural rules because routes/chat.ts:191 reads the entire `req.body.messages` array with no schema, role, or length validation and passes it verbatim to `streamText` at routes/chat.ts:206 alongside the trusted system prompt. Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable

2. Move every enforceable rule out of the prompt into server-side checks at the tool boundary, so an injected instruction cannot change what the tools will do.
3. Add a test that posts a messages array containing a `role: 'system'` entry and asserts the request is rejected with HTTP 400.

threats.title: [F-023] SSRF via profile image URL (routes/profileImageUrlUpload.ts:24)
threats.description:
A low-privilege authenticated user makes the server issue arbitrary outbound requests because routes/profileImageUrlUpload.ts:24 calls `fetch(url)` with `req.body.imageUrl` taken verbatim from routes/profileImageUrlUpload.ts:19. No scheme or host allowlist is applied, so the attacker targets loopback services, RFC 1918 addresses, or a cloud metadata endpoint. When the fetch fails, the catch branch at routes/profileImageUrlUpload.ts:36 stores the raw URL on the user profile, turning response behaviour and timing into an oracle for what the server could reach.

Impact: Internal network and cloud metadata reachable from the API server can be probed, and retrieved content is written into the publicly served uploads directory.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-918
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:

- routes/profileImageUrlUpload.ts:24

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-023 (F-023)
threats.mitigation:
M-023 — Validate and allowlist outbound request targets (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Before the fetch at routes/profileImageUrlUpload.ts:24, parse the URL, require an https scheme, resolve the host, and reject loopback, link-local, and private address ranges as well as any host outside a configured allowlist.

threats.title: [F-032] Login endpoint without rate limiting (server.ts:596)
threats.description:
An anonymous attacker runs unbounded credential stuffing against `POST /rest/user/login` because server.ts:596 registers the route with only `login()` and no throttling middleware. Rate limiting is applied in this file at server.ts:343 for password reset and at server.ts:459, 466, and 472 for the 2FA routes, and nowhere else, so the primary authentication endpoint is the one credential-guessing surface with no bound. Each attempt also runs the raw SQL query at routes/login.ts:34, so the load falls straight on SQLite.

Impact: Unlimited password guessing against every account and sustained database load from an anonymous source, with no lockout and no logged evidence.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-307
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
server.ts:596 registers the login route with no rate-limiting middleware, while rateLimit is demonstrably applied on four other routes in the same file.
- server.ts:596

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-2 external → auth-service (internet-facing): The boundary assumes credential endpoints throttle by IP and account, but the login handler applies no limiter at all on either dimension.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-032 (F-032)
threats.mitigation:
M-032 — Rate-limit and lock out repeated authentication attempts (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Insert a rateLimit middleware ahead of `login()` at server.ts:596 keyed on both the submitted email and the true client address, backed by a shared store so the limit survives multiple processes.
2. Add progressive delay or temporary lockout after repeated failures for the same account, and emit a throttling event to the audit sink.
3. Add a test issuing repeated failed logins for one account and asserting HTTP 429 once the threshold is crossed.
Verification: Issue login attempts above the configured threshold for one email from one source and assert the excess requests return HTTP 429 and no database query is executed.
Reference: CWE-307: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts

threats.title: [F-033] Unbounded LLM token consumption (server.ts:638)
threats.description:
LLM10 — Unbounded Consumption: an anonymous attacker drives arbitrary spend at the external LLM provider because server.ts:638 registers `POST /rest/chat` with neither authentication nor rate limiting. routes/chat.ts:206 forwards the caller-supplied message array with no size cap and no output-token limit, while `stopWhen: stepCountIs(10)` at routes/chat.ts:209 permits ten model round-trips per request and `maxRetries` at routes/chat.ts:208 multiplies each of them. Concurrent requests carrying maximal message payloads therefore consume provider quota and server sockets without bound.

Impact: Provider quota exhaustion and cost escalation from anonymous traffic, plus long-lived SSE connections that starve the single Express process serving all REST, WebSocket, and static traffic.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-400
CVSS v4: 8.7 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
server.ts:638 registers the chat route with no auth or throttle middleware, and routes/chat.ts:206 passes the unbounded caller message array to streamText with no maxOutputTokens setting.
- server.ts:638

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-033 (F-033)
threats.mitigation:
M-033 — Rate-limit expensive requests and bound input size (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Add `security.isAuthorized()` and a per-identity rateLimit middleware to the route registration at server.ts:638 so anonymous callers cannot reach the provider at all.
2. Set an explicit `maxOutputTokens` on the streamText call at routes/chat.ts:203 and reject request bodies whose total message length exceeds a configured character budget.
3. Add a test that posts an oversized message array and asserts HTTP 413 before any provider call is attempted.
Verification: POST /rest/chat anonymously and assert HTTP 401; then post an over-budget message array with a valid token and assert HTTP 413 with the provider client spy showing zero calls.

threats.title: [F-034] Rate limiter bypassable via forwarded header (server.ts:346)
threats.description:
An attacker defeats the only password-reset throttle because the `keyGenerator` at server.ts:346 buckets requests by `headers['X-Forwarded-For'] ?? ip`, a value the client fully controls. With `app.enable('trust proxy')` set at server.ts:342 and no trusted-proxy allowlist, rotating the header on each request places every attempt in a fresh bucket, so the 100-request window configured at server.ts:344-345 never triggers. The reset handler at routes/resetPassword.ts:41 then permits unlimited security-answer guessing, and a correct guess sets a new password at routes/resetPassword.ts:44.

Impact: Unlimited brute forcing of security answers leading to password reset and account takeover, with the intended throttle providing no protection.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-693
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
server.ts:346 derives the rate-limit key from the client-supplied X-Forwarded-For header rather than from a proxy-validated address.
- server.ts:346

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-034 (F-034)
threats.mitigation:
M-034 — Key the reset-password limiter on the proxy-validated address (priority P2, effort Low)
1. Remove the custom keyGenerator at server.ts:346 so express-rate-limit uses `req.ip`, and configure `app.set('trust proxy', ...)` at server.ts:342 with the specific hop count or address of the deployment's reverse proxy instead of the blanket enable.
2. Add a second limiter dimension keyed on the submitted email so one account cannot be attacked from many sources.
3. Add a test issuing over-threshold reset attempts while rotating X-Forwarded-For and asserting HTTP 429.
Verification: Send 150 POSTs to /rest/user/reset-password from one source with a unique X-Forwarded-For value each time and assert requests beyond the threshold return HTTP 429.
Reference: CWE-693: Protection Mechanism Failure

threats.title: [F-035] Coupon discount unbounded server-side (routes/chat.ts:184)
threats.description:
LLM06 — Excessive Agency: routes/chat.ts:184 issues a real, redeemable coupon from a discount value the model chose, with no server-side bound and no authorization of the caller. The tool's input schema at routes/chat.ts:179 declares `z.number()` with the ten percent cap stated only in the description text and in the prompt policy at routes/chat.ts:98-103, so nothing outside the prompt constrains the value. Combined with the unauthenticated route at server.ts:638 and the unvalidated message array at routes/chat.ts:191, an anonymous caller injects an instruction that makes the model call the tool with an arbitrary discount.

Impact: An anonymous attacker mints coupons at any discount percentage, redeemable at checkout, converting a prompt-level policy into unbounded revenue loss.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-862
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
routes/chat.ts:184 calls security.generateCoupon with the model-supplied discount; the schema at line 179 imposes no maximum and no code path validates the value before issuance.
- routes/chat.ts:184

threats.mitigation:

threats.title: [F-036] Deluxe role granted without payment (routes/deluxe.ts:43)

A customer promotes themselves to the deluxe role for free because routes/deluxe.ts:43 updates the user's role and issues a matching `deluxeToken` unconditionally after the two payment branches. threats.title: [F-048] Confidential policy in LLM system prompt (routes/chat.ts:105)

Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable

Verification: Re-run the IAC-050 scanner check; it reports no match at package-lock.json:0, and the regression test passes.

data.name: Authentication and Session Service
data.description: JWT-based authentication, TOTP 2FA setup and verification, password management, and OAuth implicit flow handlers co-located on the Express server. Core signing and validation logic lives in lib/insecurity.ts; route handlers in routes/login.ts, routes/2fa.ts, and related files implement the application trust boundary.

threats.title: [F-011] Password reset accepts a security-question answer routes/resetPassword.ts:10
threats.description:
An attacker who can research or guess the answer can satisfy the recovery check and take over the account without the original credential.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-640
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: source-scan

Evidence:
- routes/resetPassword.ts:10

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-011 (F-011)
threats.mitigation:
M-011 — Replace security-question recovery with a CSPRNG reset token delivered through… (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Replace security-question recovery with a CSPRNG reset token delivered through a verified out-of-band channel; expire it quickly and invalidate it after one use.
2. Add a regression test (or CI check) that fails on the vulnerable pattern and passes once the fix is in place.
Verification: Re-run the AUTHN-001 scanner check; it reports no match at routes/resetPassword.ts:10, and the regression test passes.

threats.title: [F-018] Non-cryptographic RNG for a secret/token lib/insecurity.ts:53
threats.description:
A predictable token/secret lets an attacker guess or brute-force session identifiers, reset links, or OTPs.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-330
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: source-scan

Evidence:
- lib/insecurity.ts:53

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-018 (F-018)
threats.mitigation:
M-018 — Use cryptographically secure random values (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Use crypto.randomBytes / crypto.randomUUID / webcrypto getRandomValues for any security value.
2. Add a regression test (or CI check) that fails on the vulnerable pattern and passes once the fix is in place.
Verification: Re-run the CRYPTO-002 scanner check; it reports no match at lib/insecurity.ts:53, and the regression test passes.

threats.title: [F-024] Unbounded field selection leaks credentials (routes/currentUser.ts:31)
threats.description:
An attacker hosts a page that loads GET /rest/user/whoami?fields=password,totpSecret&callback=steal as a script; the victim browser attaches the token cookie the endpoint reads at routes/currentUser.ts:17, the loop at line 31 copies whichever user attributes were named into the response, and line 58 returns them as executable JSONP to the attacker origin.

Impact: The victim's MD5 password hash and TOTP shared secret leave the application to an attacker-controlled origin, giving offline password recovery and the ability to generate valid second-factor codes for that account.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-200
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
routes/currentUser.ts:31 assigns baseUser[field] from user.data for every comma-separated name in the fields query parameter with no allowlist, and line 58 serves that object via res.jsonp when a callback parameter is present.
- routes/currentUser.ts:31

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-024 (F-024)
threats.mitigation:
M-024 — Stop exposing internal information to clients (priority P2, effort Low)
1. At routes/currentUser.ts:31 intersect the requested field names against the fixed set id, email, lastLoginIp and profileImage and discard any other name.
2. Remove the res.jsonp branch at routes/currentUser.ts:58 so the cookie-authenticated response can no longer be read cross-origin as a script.
3. Add tests asserting that fields=password and fields=totpSecret are absent from the response body and that a callback parameter yields application/json rather than JavaScript.
Verification: Run the new tests: GET /rest/user/whoami?fields=password,totpSecret returns a body without password or totpSecret keys, and ?callback=x returns Content-Type application/json.
Reference: CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

threats.title: [F-025] MD5 password hashing (lib/insecurity.ts:41)
threats.description:
An attacker who obtains the Users table through the login SQL injection or the whoami field selector runs the recovered digests through a commodity MD5 cracking rig, recovering the plaintext passwords of every account because lib/insecurity.ts:41 hashes credentials with a single unsalted MD5 pass.

Impact: Recovered plaintext passwords expose every user account and enable credential reuse against unrelated services, converting a single database read into a permanent, application-wide credential compromise.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-328
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
lib/insecurity.ts:41 defines the password hash as crypto.createHash('md5').update(data).digest('hex') with no salt and no work factor, and routes/login.ts:34, routes/2fa.ts:107 and routes/changePassword.ts:39 all compare against that digest.
- lib/insecurity.ts:41

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-025 (F-025)
threats.mitigation:
M-025 — Use modern cryptographic hash and KDF algorithms (priority P2, effort High)
1. Introduce a bcrypt or Argon2id hash and verify helper alongside lib/insecurity.ts:41 with sound parameters, and reject password input above the algorithm's UTF-8 byte limit at set and change time.
2. Migrate stored digests by rehashing on next successful login and retiring the MD5 comparison in routes/login.ts, routes/2fa.ts and routes/changePassword.ts once migration completes.
3. Add a test that registers a user and asserts the stored password field carries the new algorithm prefix and is not a 32-character hexadecimal string.
Verification: Run the new test: after registration the persisted password column matches the bcrypt or Argon2 identifier prefix and does not match ^[0-9a-f]{32}$.
Reference: CWE-328: Use of Weak Hash

threats.title: [F-037] Unverified password change (routes/changePassword.ts:39)
threats.description:
An attacker holding any valid token for a victim, whether forged with the in-source signing key or captured through the JSONP whoami leak, calls the change-password endpoint without a current parameter; the guard at routes/changePassword.ts:39 only runs when currentPassword is truthy, so the update at line 51 proceeds and the attacker sets a password of their choosing.

Impact: Any leaked or forged session token converts into permanent ownership of the victim account, including administrative accounts, because the legitimate owner is locked out and the attacker retains a password they chose.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-620
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
routes/changePassword.ts:39 wraps the current-password comparison in an if (currentPassword && ...) condition, so omitting the current query parameter skips verification entirely before user.update at line 51 writes the new password.
- routes/changePassword.ts:39

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-037 (F-037)
threats.mitigation:
M-037 — Require and verify the current password (priority P2, effort Low)
1. Reject the request with 401 when currentPassword is absent at routes/changePassword.ts:39, then compare it against loggedInUser.data.password unconditionally.
2. Invalidate the caller's other sessions after a successful change by removing the corresponding authenticatedUsers entries.
3. Add a test asserting that a change-password request without a current parameter returns 401 and leaves the stored password unchanged.
Verification: Run the new test: a change-password request with a valid token but no current parameter returns HTTP 401 and the persisted password hash is byte-identical before and after.
Reference: CWE-620: Unverified Password Change

threats.title: [F-038] Security-question password recovery (routes/resetPassword.ts:41)
threats.description:
An unauthenticated attacker posts a victim email with candidate security answers to /rest/user/reset-password; routes/resetPassword.ts:41 compares only an HMAC of the submitted answer against the stored value, with no proof of mailbox ownership, no second factor and no attempt limit, so a researched or guessed answer sets a new password at line 44.

Impact: Any account whose security answer is guessable or discoverable from public sources, including administrative accounts, is taken over by an unauthenticated internet caller without touching the victim's password or second factor.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-640
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
routes/resetPassword.ts:41 gates the password update solely on security.hmac(answer) matching the stored answer for the account identified by the submitted email, and the request never proves control of that mailbox.
- routes/resetPassword.ts:41

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-2 external → auth-service (internet-facing): An unauthenticated caller crossing this boundary changes an account password using only a knowledge answer, with no credential verification and no throttle.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-038 (F-038)
threats.mitigation:
M-038 — Replace security-answer recovery with an emailed single-use reset token (priority P2, effort High)
1. Replace the answer comparison at routes/resetPassword.ts:41 with verification of a short-lived single-use token generated by crypto.randomBytes and delivered only to the registered address, never returned in the response body or URL.
2. Keep the response non-enumerating so an unknown email and a known email produce the same status and timing, and apply the shared-store rate limiter from the login remediation to this route.
3. Add tests asserting the reset response body and logs contain no token, that a token is single-use, and that it expires.
Verification: Run the new tests: the reset-request response body contains no token value, replaying a consumed token returns 401, and a token used after its TTL returns 401.
Reference: CWE-640: Weak Password Recovery Mechanism for Forgotten Password

threats.title: [F-052] Password in URL query string (routes/changePassword.ts:15)
threats.description:
A user changes their password and the current and new plaintext passwords travel in the request URL, because routes/changePassword.ts reads them from query.current and query.new; anyone with access to reverse-proxy access logs, browser history, or a Referer header captured by a third-party asset on the page recovers those credentials verbatim.

Impact: Plaintext passwords are persisted in infrastructure logs and browser history outside the application's control, so a log reader or a compromised third-party script recovers working credentials for the affected accounts.

Risk: Medium (likelihood High, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-598
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
routes/changePassword.ts:15 reads the new password from query.new and line 14 reads the current password from query.current, so both credentials are carried in the request line rather than a request body.
- routes/changePassword.ts:15

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-052 (F-052)
threats.mitigation:
M-052 — Move password-change credentials from the query string to the request body (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Change the handler at routes/changePassword.ts to read current, new and repeat from req.body and register the route as POST, updating the Angular client that calls it.
2. Reject any request that still carries these values as query parameters so a stale client cannot keep leaking them.
3. Add a test asserting that a password change succeeds with a body payload and returns 400 when the credentials are supplied as query parameters.
Verification: Run the new test: POST /rest/user/change-password with a JSON body succeeds, and the same values passed as query parameters return HTTP 400.
Reference: CWE-598: Use of GET Request Method With Sensitive Query Strings

threats.title: [F-062] Unbounded session token map (lib/insecurity.ts:74)
threats.description:
An attacker repeatedly authenticates or replays distinct valid tokens; each one is inserted into the process-local tokenMap at lib/insecurity.ts:74, which has no size cap, no expiry sweep and no removal on logout, so resident memory grows monotonically until the Node process is killed by the allocator.

Impact: Sustained token insertion exhausts heap memory and terminates the authentication process, taking down login for all users; the same map also retains full user records for sessions that were never revoked.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-400
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
lib/insecurity.ts:74 writes this.tokenMap[token] = user with no eviction, and updateAuthenticatedUsers at line 191 inserts any externally supplied token that verifies, including one presented through the token cookie read at line 187.
- lib/insecurity.ts:74

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-062 (F-062)
threats.mitigation:
M-062 — Rate-limit expensive requests and bound input size (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Replace the plain object at lib/insecurity.ts:74 with a bounded LRU or TTL cache whose entry lifetime matches the 6h token expiry, and delete entries on logout and on password change.
2. Cap the map size and reject insertion beyond the cap rather than growing without limit.
3. Add a test that inserts more entries than the configured cap and asserts the map size stays at or below the cap and that an expired entry is no longer resolvable.
Verification: Run the new test: after inserting cap+1 tokens the map reports at most cap entries, and a token advanced past its TTL resolves to undefined.
Reference: CWE-400: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption

data.name: SQLite Database
data.description: SQLite 3 data store (default) holding user accounts, orders, basket items, product catalog, feedback, payment cards, addresses, and challenge state. Accessed via TypeORM entity models; the runtime database file is created and seeded at startup by data/datacreator.ts.

threats.title: [F-005] Hard-coded seeded account credentials (data/datacreator.ts:196)
threats.description:
An attacker reads the shipped static user data, then authenticates as the seeded administrator because createUsers writes the configured password verbatim into the Users table at every startup, giving full application authority without any credential guess.

Impact: Full compromise of the persisted data set: user accounts, orders, basket items, payment cards, addresses, and wallet balances are readable and modifiable by anyone holding the shipped credential.

Risk: Critical (likelihood High, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-798
CVSS v4: 9.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:L/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
createUsers loads records through loadStaticUserData (data/datacreator.ts:187) and passes the static password field straight into UserModel.create at line 196, so the seeded credential is fixed for every deployment of this build.
- data/datacreator.ts:196

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-005 (F-005)
threats.mitigation:
M-005 — Move secrets to a managed secret store (priority P1, effort Medium)
1. In createUsers (data/datacreator.ts:186-202), stop persisting the static password field: require each seeded account password from external configuration at startup, or generate one per account with crypto.randomBytes and disclose it once through an operator-only channel.
2. Add a seeding test that asserts no persisted User row hashes a password value present in the static user data file.
Verification: Run the seeding routine twice against fresh databases and compare the two admin password column values; they must differ, and neither may equal the hash of the static configured password.
Reference: CWE-798: Use of Hard-coded Credentials

threats.title: [F-014] Plaintext TOTP secret column (models/user.ts:112)
threats.description:
An attacker who obtains read access to the database file or to any query result exposing the Users table reads the totpSecret column verbatim and generates valid second-factor codes for the affected account, defeating two-factor authentication without touching the victim's device.

Impact: Two-factor authentication no longer adds a barrier once the database file leaks: an attacker with a cracked or reset password mints valid codes and reaches accounts holding orders, payment cards, and wallet balances.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-311
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
The User model declares totpSecret as a plain DataTypes.STRING with no setter, hash, or encryption wrapper (models/user.ts:112-115), unlike the password and security-answer columns which pass through a transform, so the shared secret is persisted exactly as issued.
- models/user.ts:112

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-014 (F-014)
threats.mitigation:
M-014 — Encrypt the totpSecret column (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Add a setter on the totpSecret attribute in models/user.ts that encrypts the value with an AEAD cipher keyed from external secret configuration, and a matching getter that decrypts on read.
2. Add a model test that creates a user with a known TOTP seed and asserts the raw persisted column value does not contain that seed.
Verification: Create a user with a known TOTP seed, then query the Users table directly and confirm the totpSecret column does not equal the seed.
Reference: CWE-311: Missing Encryption of Sensitive Data

threats.title: [F-022] Legacy sanitizer on persisted username (models/user.ts:49)
threats.description:
An attacker submits markup in the username field and the User model persists it after passing it through sanitizeLegacy instead of sanitizeSecure, so the stored row keeps payload that the weaker filter does not remove and that every later consumer of the username reads back as markup.

Impact: Stored markup in user-controlled columns is served back to other users and administrators, which can hijack their sessions and, through an administrator session, expose the order, address, and payment card rows held in this database.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-79
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
The username setter branches on a runtime challenge flag and calls security.sanitizeLegacy at models/user.ts:49, taking a deliberately weaker path than the sanitizeSecure call on line 51; the same pattern selects the weaker sanitizeHtml at models/feedback.ts:44.
- models/user.ts:49

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-022 (F-022)
threats.mitigation:
M-022 — Encode output instead of bypassing the framework sanitizer (priority P2, effort Low)
1. Remove the challenge-flag branch in the username setter (models/user.ts:47-54) so every write passes through security.sanitizeSecure, and apply the same change to the comment setter in models/feedback.ts.
2. Add model tests that write known script and iframe payloads to username and feedback comment and assert the persisted values contain no markup.
Verification: Create a user with username '<iframe src="javascript:alert(1)">' and assert the persisted username column contains no iframe tag.
Reference: CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation

threats.title: [F-028] Plaintext payment card number storage (models/card.ts:38)
threats.description:
An attacker who reads the SQLite file, a backup copy, or any query result over the Cards table recovers complete sixteen-digit card numbers together with the cardholder name and expiry, because the model persists the full number as a plain integer with no encryption, tokenization, or truncation.

Impact: Full payment card records including holder name and expiry are exposed in one read of an unencrypted file that sits on the same filesystem as the application process, which is a direct cardholder-data breach.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-311
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
models/card.ts:38-45 declares cardNum as DataTypes.INTEGER constrained only to the sixteen-digit range, with fullName, expMonth, and expYear stored alongside it, and no setter transforms the value; a search for encryption in models/ and data/datacreator.ts returned no hit.
- models/card.ts:38

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-028 (F-028)
threats.mitigation:
M-028 — Tokenize or encrypt the cardNum column (priority P2, effort High)
1. Replace the plain cardNum attribute at models/card.ts:38 with a stored last-four digit fragment plus a token or AEAD ciphertext keyed from external secret configuration, and migrate existing rows.
2. Add a model test asserting that a created card row exposes no more than the last four digits in any queried column.
Verification: Create a card with a known number, then query the Cards table directly and confirm the full number does not appear in any column.
Reference: CWE-311: Missing Encryption of Sensitive Data

threats.title: [F-029] Unsalted fast password hash (models/user.ts:76)
threats.description:
An attacker who obtains the database file or any query result exposing the password column recovers the cleartext passwords offline, because the User model stores a single-call digest of the password with no per-user salt and no work factor, so precomputed tables apply directly.

Impact: Every account password in the store, including the administrator and accounting roles, is recoverable offline, which yields access to orders, addresses, payment cards, and wallet balances held in the same database.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-916
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
The password setter at models/user.ts:76 stores security.hash(clearTextPassword) as the whole column value, and the model declares no salt or iteration attribute anywhere in its attribute list (models/user.ts:24-33), so identical passwords produce identical stored values.
- models/user.ts:76

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-029 (F-029)
threats.mitigation:
M-029 — Hash passwords with a strong, salted algorithm (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Change the password setter at models/user.ts:76 to store a bcrypt or Argon2id hash with per-user salt and tuned cost parameters, reject password input above the algorithm's byte limit, and rehash on next successful login for existing rows.
2. Add a model test asserting two users with the same cleartext password store different column values and that the stored value carries the KDF identifier and cost parameters.
Verification: Create two users with the same password and confirm their stored password columns differ and both begin with the KDF prefix.
Reference: CWE-916: Use of Password Hash With Insufficient Computational Effort

threats.title: [F-044] Seed download without integrity check (data/datacreator.ts:390)
threats.description:
An attacker who controls the configured product image or blueprint URL, or who intercepts the fetch, supplies arbitrary bytes that the seeding routine writes straight into the served asset directory, because downloadToFile is called with no checksum, signature, or content-type verification.

Impact: Attacker-chosen content is published from the application's own asset path and the product catalog rows seeded alongside it reference it, so users receive tampered files from a trusted origin.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Low, impact High)
CWE: CWE-345
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
data/datacreator.ts:390 calls utils.downloadToFile with a remote URL and a destination under frontend/dist/frontend/assets/public/images/products/ whose filename comes from that same URL, and line 418 repeats the pattern for the blueprint file; neither call verifies the retrieved bytes.
- data/datacreator.ts:390

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-044 (F-044)
threats.mitigation:
M-044 — Verify token signatures before trusting claims (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Require a configured SHA-256 digest for every remote asset in the seeding configuration and make downloadToFile at data/datacreator.ts:390 and :418 reject a file whose computed digest does not match before it is written.
2. Add a seeding test that supplies a URL whose content does not match the declared digest and asserts no file is written to the asset directory.
Verification: Seed with a deliberately wrong digest configured for one product image and confirm the seed run logs a rejection and the target file is absent from the asset directory.
Reference: CWE-345: Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity

threats.title: [F-065] Unbounded persisted text growth (models/feedback.ts:40)
threats.description:
An attacker submits very large comment bodies repeatedly and grows the single SQLite file until the host filesystem fills, because the comment column declares no length validator and SQLite does not enforce the declared string type, so nothing bounds the bytes written per row.

Impact: A full filesystem makes the shared database unwritable for every user and the application cannot recover on its own, taking down ordering, authentication, and all state held in the store.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-400
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
models/feedback.ts:39-56 declares comment as DataTypes.STRING with a sanitizing setter but no validate block, while models/address.ts:55 and :61 show the project's own len validator pattern being applied elsewhere; the store is a single file at models/index.ts:41 and the retry policy at models/index.ts:36 matches only SQLITE_BUSY.
- models/feedback.ts:40

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-065 (F-065)
threats.mitigation:
M-065 — Rate-limit expensive requests and bound input size (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Add a validate len bound to the comment attribute in models/feedback.ts and to the equivalent free-text attributes on the complaint and memory models, matching the len pattern already used in models/address.ts.
2. Add a model test asserting that a create call with an oversized comment is rejected by validation rather than persisted.
Verification: Attempt to create a feedback row with a comment above the configured limit and confirm the create rejects with a Sequelize validation error and no row is written.
Reference: CWE-400: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption

threats.title: [F-068] No database principal separation (models/index.ts:33)
threats.description:
An attacker who reaches any query path, including one opened by an injection flaw elsewhere in the process, operates with full authority over every table, because a single Sequelize connection created once at module load serves all access levels and SQLite enforces no per-principal or row-level permission.

Impact: There is no containment boundary inside the store: a flaw on any single query path yields read and write access to credentials, payment cards, addresses, orders, and wallet balances alike.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-284
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
createSequelize at models/index.ts:33-44 builds one connection against the file store and initModels binds all twenty-one entities to that single instance at line 75, so no read-only, per-role, or per-tenant connection exists anywhere in the persistence layer.
- models/index.ts:33

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-068 (F-068)
threats.mitigation:
M-068 — Apply least-privilege filesystem access (priority P3, effort High)
1. Introduce scoped repository functions over the shared Sequelize instance in models/index.ts that apply a mandatory owner or role predicate to every query touching Users, Cards, Addresses, Baskets, and Wallets, and forbid direct model access from route code, or migrate to an engine that supports database roles and row-level security.
2. Add tests that call each scoped repository function as a non-owning user and assert an empty result or a rejection.
Verification: Call the card and address repository functions with a user id that does not own the row and confirm no row is returned.
Reference: CWE-284: Improper Access Control

data.name: GitHub Actions CI/CD Pipeline
data.description: GitHub Actions workflows providing CI (build, test, code coverage), release (npm publish, Docker image), and CodeQL security scanning. Actions are referenced by tag only (not SHA-pinned), and workflows default to write-all repository permissions.

threats.title: [F-012] Unsigned container publish (.github/workflows/ci.yml:327)
threats.description:
An attacker who obtains the DOCKERHUB_TOKEN repository secret authenticates at .github/workflows/ci.yml:327 and pushes a backdoored image over the bkimminich/juice-shop:latest tag written on line 345. No step in any workflow signs the image or emits a provenance attestation, so a downstream `docker pull` cannot distinguish the attacker's image from a genuine pipeline build.

Impact: Consumers pulling bkimminich/juice-shop:latest execute attacker-supplied code under the project's own name, with no cryptographic means to detect the substitution and no way to bind a published image back to a specific pipeline run.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-345
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
ci.yml:327 authenticates the Docker Hub push with the long-lived DOCKERHUB_TOKEN repository secret rather than a workflow-scoped OIDC credential, and no workflow under .github/workflows requests id-token, invokes cosign, or produces a provenance attestation.
- .github/workflows/ci.yml:327

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-012 (F-012)
threats.mitigation:
M-012 — Verify token signatures before trusting claims (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Add `permissions: id-token: write` to the docker job in .github/workflows/ci.yml and exchange the OIDC token for a short-lived Docker Hub credential instead of passing secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN on line 327.
2. Set `provenance: true` and `sbom: true` on the docker/build-push-action step at line 338, and add a cosign keyless signing step for the pushed digest.
3. Add a release smoke check that runs `cosign verify` against the published tag and fails the workflow when verification does not succeed.
Verification: Run `cosign verify --certificate-identity-regexp 'github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop' --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com bkimminich/juice-shop:latest` and expect a successful verification against the pipeline identity.
Reference: https://slsa.dev/spec/v1.0/provenance

threats.title: [F-019] Action pinned to mutable branch ref (.github/workflows/image_actions.yml:33)
threats.description:
Whoever controls the main branch of calibreapp/image-actions pushes a commit that GitHub resolves the next time .github/workflows/image_actions.yml:33 runs, executing that code inside this repository's runner with the secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN handed to it on line 35. A branch reference is re-resolved on every run, so no review of the repository can pin what actually executes.

Impact: Arbitrary third-party code executes in the repository's CI with a repository-scoped GITHUB_TOKEN, allowing modification of source and workflow files that subsequently flow into the published Docker image and the packaged release archive.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-1104
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
image_actions.yml:33 references calibreapp/image-actions@main, a mutable branch ref that GitHub re-resolves on every run, and line 35 passes secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN to it. threats.title: [F-020] Release built without dependency lockfile (.github/workflows/release.yml:55)

The package's install hook executes on the runner and its code is packaged by `npm run package:ci` on line 56 into the archive that softprops/action-gh-release attaches to the release on line 58.

Impact: Every published release archive and Docker image can carry code that was never reviewed in a pull request, and the absence of a lockfile means no diff signal exists to detect the substitution after the fact.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-1357
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
release.yml:55 installs with `npm install --production`, which resolves versions against the current registry state and executes lifecycle scripts. No package-lock.json exists in the repository and no workflow under .github/workflows uses `npm ci`, so no build in the pipeline is reproducible from a committed dependency baseline.
- .github/workflows/release.yml:55

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-020 (F-020)
threats.mitigation:
M-020 — Set least-privilege CI workflow permissions (priority P2, effort Medium)

2. Add a minimum release age gate (npm `--before` or a Renovate `minimumReleaseAge` policy) so a version published minutes earlier cannot enter a release build.
3. Add a CI job that runs `npm ci` twice and fails if the lockfile is modified, proving the release install is deterministic.

threats.title: [F-026] Bot PAT exposed to later steps (.github/workflows/update-challenges-www.yml:19)
threats.description:
The checkout at .github/workflows/update-challenges-www.yml:19 authenticates with secrets.BOT_TOKEN, a token carrying write access to the separate repository juice-shop/juice-shop.github.io, and does not set persist-credentials: false, so actions/checkout writes that token into the workspace .git/config as an HTTP extraheader. Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-522
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
update-challenges-www.yml:19 passes secrets.BOT_TOKEN to actions/checkout for the external repository juice-shop/juice-shop.github.io. No workflow under .github/workflows sets persist-credentials: false, and lines 28 and 37 interpolate ${{ github.ref_name }} into a run: shell block. The same BOT_TOKEN pattern repeats in update-challenges-www-legacy.yml:19, update-challenges-ebook.yml:18, update-news-www.yml:14 and update-news-www-legacy.yml:14.

2. Replace the long-lived BOT_TOKEN personal access token with a GitHub App installation token minted per run and scoped to the single target repository and the single content path it writes.
3. Move ${{ github.ref_name }} out of the `run:` command lines on lines 28 and 37 into an `env:` entry and reference it as "$REF_NAME", so a branch name can no longer alter the command.

threats.title: [F-039] Comment command without author authorization (.github/workflows/rebase.yml:10)
threats.description:
Any GitHub user who can comment on a pull request triggers the privileged rebase job, because the condition at .github/workflows/rebase.yml:10 tests only that the thread is a pull request and that the comment body contains `/rebase`, and never checks github.event.comment.author_association or the commenter's repository permission. The issue_comment event runs the workflow from the default branch with repository secrets and the GITHUB_TOKEN passed to cirrus-actions/rebase on line 19, which fetches the pull request head and force-pushes a rewritten branch.

Impact: An account with no repository permission causes a privileged, secrets-bearing job to run on demand and to force-push a rewritten branch, which both crosses the pipeline's authorization boundary and gives an attacker a repeatable trigger for any weakness that later appears in that job.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-862
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
rebase.yml:10 gates the job only on `github.event.issue.pull_request != '' && contains(github.event.comment.body, '/rebase')`. The workflow declares no permissions block and passes secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN to the rebase action on line 19, and no workflow under .github/workflows references author_association.
- .github/workflows/rebase.yml:10

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-039 (F-039)
threats.mitigation:
M-039 — Enforce server-side authorization on every endpoint (priority P2, effort Low)
1. Extend the condition at .github/workflows/rebase.yml:10 to require `contains(fromJSON('["OWNER","MEMBER","COLLABORATOR"]'), github.event.comment.author_association)` so only privileged commenters trigger the job.
2. Add an explicit `permissions: contents: write` block to the rebase job so the token is not issued with the repository default scope.
3. Add a concurrency group keyed on the issue number so repeated `/rebase` comments cannot queue parallel rebases of the same branch.
Verification: Comment `/rebase` from an account with no repository permission and confirm the rebase job is skipped while the workflow run itself still completes via always_job.
Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/862.html

threats.title: [F-043] Remote installer executed without integrity check (.github/workflows/ci.yml:358)
threats.description:
An attacker who controls the cli-assets.heroku.com distribution point serves a modified install.sh, which .github/workflows/ci.yml:358 pipes straight into sh with no checksum, signature, or pinned version. The script executes in the heroku job that goes on to deploy production with secrets.HEROKU_API_KEY on line 371, so the substituted code both runs on the runner and can read the deployment credential.

Impact: Substituted installer code runs on the deployment runner and reaches the Heroku API key, which deploys the master branch to the production juice-shop application, so a single upstream compromise reaches the production deployment.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Low, impact High)
CWE: CWE-829
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
ci.yml:358 runs `curl https://cli-assets.heroku.com/install.sh | sh` with no checksum verification, signature check, or version pin, inside the same job that consumes secrets.HEROKU_API_KEY at line 371 to deploy to Heroku.
- .github/workflows/ci.yml:358

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-043 (F-043)
threats.mitigation:
M-043 — Pin third-party dependencies to immutable versions (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Replace the piped installer at .github/workflows/ci.yml:358 with a pinned tarball download plus a `sha256sum -c` check against a checksum committed to the repository, or install the CLI from a SHA-pinned action.
2. Move the Heroku deploy step into its own job so the installer step never shares a job environment with secrets.HEROKU_API_KEY.
3. Add a workflow test that flips one byte of the expected checksum and confirms the job fails before the deploy step runs.
Verification: Run the heroku job with a deliberately wrong expected SHA-256 and confirm the run fails at the install step with a checksum mismatch and never reaches `akhileshns/heroku-deploy`.

threats.title: [F-046] Unsigned CI commit to trunk (.github/workflows/frontend-bundle-analysis.yml:61)
threats.description:
The bundle-analysis job sets its committer to a synthetic `GitHub Action <action@github.com>` identity at .github/workflows/frontend-bundle-analysis.yml:61 and then commits and pushes to master on line 66 without a commit signature. An attacker with any write path into the repository can commit under identical author and committer fields, and a reviewer reading the master history has no signature or account link that distinguishes the pipeline's commit from the forged one.
