Impact: Commits reaching the trunk cannot be attributed to an accountable principal, so a forensic review after a suspected pipeline compromise cannot separate genuine automated commits from forged ones, and a rejected push produces no failing run to investigate.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-778
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
frontend-bundle-analysis.yml:61-62 configures a committer name and e-mail that map to no GitHub account, line 66 pushes that commit to master, and line 67 marks the push step continue-on-error. No workflow under .github/workflows configures GPG or SSH commit signing.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-046 (F-046)

M-046 — Add security audit logging (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Replace the synthetic identity at .github/workflows/frontend-bundle-analysis.yml:61-62 with the account-linked JuiceShopBot identity already used by the update-* workflows, and import a signing key so `git commit -S` produces a verified commit.
2. Remove `continue-on-error: true` from line 67 so a rejected or failed push to master fails the workflow run.

Verification: Trigger the workflow via workflow_dispatch and confirm the resulting master commit shows as Verified in the GitHub UI and that a forced push failure marks the run as failed.

threats.title: [F-063] Unbounded CI fan-out on pull requests (.github/workflows/ci.yml:14)
threats.description:
Any internet user can open and then repeatedly update a pull request against the public repository, and the pull_request trigger at .github/workflows/ci.yml:14 starts frontend-test, server-test and api-test, each a three-operating-system by three-Node-version matrix whose test steps retry up to three times, alongside the e2e, smoke, docker-test and custom-config jobs. The workflow declares no concurrency group, so each new commit the attacker pushes queues another full set of runners instead of cancelling the previous run.

Impact: Actions concurrency and billed minutes for the juice-shop organisation are exhausted by attacker-controlled pull request activity, delaying or blocking the release, Docker publish and Heroku deploy jobs that depend on the same runner pool.

CWE: CWE-400
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
ci.yml:14 registers the pull_request trigger with no fork or author restriction, lines 56-59, 95-98 and 132-135 define three-by-three matrices for three separate jobs, the nick-invision/retry steps allow three attempts each, and the file contains no concurrency key at workflow or job level.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-063 (F-063)

M-063 — Rate-limit expensive requests and bound input size (priority P3, effort Low)

data.name: Real-time WebSocket Channel
data.description: Server-side socket.io real-time channel pushing live events to connected browsers. Internet-facing WebSocket surface with its own connection auth/origin checks and message-handler trust boundary.

threats.title: [F-013] Unauthenticated WebSocket Channel
threats.description:
An attacker points a non-browser Socket.IO client at port 3000 and completes the handshake without presenting any credential. The server constructs the Socket.IO server with a single `cors.origin` option and registers no handshake authentication, and CORS is a browser-enforced response header rather than a server-side admission check, so a scripted client bypasses it entirely and is accepted onto the push channel as an anonymous peer indistinguishable from the legitimate Angular frontend.

Impact: Any internet client reaches the live event channel of the same process that serves the JWT-protected REST API on port 3000, gaining read access to challenge notifications and write access to the event handlers that mutate challenge and notification state.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-306
CVSS v4: 6.9 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:L/VI:L/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts:20 constructs the Socket.IO server with `cors: { origin: 'http://localhost:4200' }` as its only connection-level option, and the connection handler at line 23 runs for every socket without inspecting a credential. A grep of both component files for `io.use(`, `allowRequest`, `handshake`, `verifyToken`, `isAuthorized`, and `authenticate` returned zero hits, so no handshake credential is verified anywhere on this channel.
- lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts:20

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-1 external → api-server (internet-facing): The Socket.IO server is attached to the same Express HTTP server the boundary protects, but the handshake bypasses the security.isAuthorized() expressJwt leg entirely.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-013 (F-013)
threats.mitigation:
M-013 — Require authentication on every exposed endpoint (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Register an `io.use()` handshake middleware in lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts that reads the token from `socket.handshake.auth` and verifies it with the same JWT verification helper `lib/insecurity.ts` supplies to `security.isAuthorized()`, calling `next(new Error('unauthorized'))` when verification fails so the connection is refused before `io.on('connection')` runs.
2. Attach the verified principal to `socket.data` and make the event handlers below it read identity from there instead of from client payloads.
3. Replace the hardcoded `http://localhost:4200` origin with a configured allow-list, and keep the origin check as defence in depth rather than as the admission control.
4. Add an integration test that opens a socket.io-client connection with no token and with a tampered token, and asserts the connection is rejected and no 'challenge solved' event is received.
Verification: Run `npx wscat -c 'ws://localhost:3000/socket.io/?EIO=4&transport=websocket'` with no auth payload and confirm the server closes the connection with an unauthorized error instead of emitting 'server started' or 'challenge solved'.
Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/306.html

threats.title: [F-021] Client-trusted security decision (lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts:41)
threats.description:
An attacker emits a `verifyLocalXssChallenge` event whose payload is simply the literal string the server searches for. The handler passes that client-supplied value directly into `challengeUtils.solveIf`, which treats a substring match on attacker-controlled data as proof that the XSS payload actually rendered in a victim browser, and then persists `solved = true`. The same pattern applies to `verifySvgInjectionChallenge` and `verifyCloseNotificationsChallenge`, so an attacker forges completion of security exercises without triggering the underlying vulnerability at all.

Impact: Challenge and scoreboard state, the integrity signal this application exists to produce, can be written by any anonymous client, so recorded training progress and CTF scoring no longer reflect actual exploitation.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-807
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts:41 passes the raw event payload `data` into `utils.contains(data, '<iframe src="javascript:alert(`xss`)">')` as the completion criterion, and line 50 accepts any client array of length greater than one. The criterion is evaluated over data the client fully controls, and lib/challengeUtils.ts:31 shows the resulting `solve()` call persists the state with `await challenge.save()`.
- lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts:41

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-021 (F-021)
threats.mitigation:
M-021 — Use trusted client IPs for rate limiting (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Derive challenge completion from server-observed state rather than a client assertion: record the XSS and SVG-injection evidence where the server already handles the request that renders or redirects, and have that server-side path call `challengeUtils.solveIf`.
2. Where a browser-side signal is genuinely unavoidable, bind the event to the authenticated socket principal from the handshake middleware and to a server-generated nonce issued for that specific attempt, and reject events whose nonce was not issued or was already consumed.
3. Add a negative test that emits verifyLocalXssChallenge with the literal payload string over a socket that never triggered the XSS, and asserts the challenge remains unsolved.
Verification: Emit `verifyLocalXssChallenge` with the literal iframe payload from a standalone socket.io-client script, then query the challenges table and assert `solved` is still false for `localXssChallenge`.
Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/807.html

threats.title: [F-027] Secret exposure to anonymous client (lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts:30)
threats.description:
An attacker opens an unauthenticated socket and the connection handler immediately replays the entire queued `notifications` array to it. Each notification carries the challenge CTF flag generated by `utils.ctfFlag`, and the `hidden` field that is meant to suppress display when `challenges.showSolvedNotifications` is off is only a rendering hint the client is trusted to honour, so notifications the operator configured as hidden are still transmitted in full to any peer that connects.

Impact: CTF flags and solved-challenge details, the credential material this application issues for scoring, are readable by any anonymous internet client, and the configured suppression of solved-challenge notifications is defeated because suppression happens only in the browser.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-200
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts:30 emits every entry of the shared `notifications` array to each newly connected socket without any authorization check. lib/challengeUtils.ts:52 shows each notification is built with `const flag = utils.ctfFlag(challenge.name)`, line 67 sets `hidden` from configuration while still including the flag in the payload, and line 75 broadcasts the same object to all connected sockets.
- lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts:30

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-027 (F-027)
threats.mitigation:
M-027 — Stop exposing internal information to clients (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Gate the replay loop at lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts:30 on the principal established by the handshake middleware, and emit nothing to a socket that carries no verified identity.
2. Build the outbound notification server-side so the `flag` field is omitted entirely when the recipient is not entitled to it, and drop the notification instead of sending it with `hidden: true` when `challenges.showSolvedNotifications` is disabled, in lib/challengeUtils.ts:62-70.
3. Add a test that connects an unauthorized socket and asserts no received 'challenge solved' payload contains a `flag` property.
Verification: Connect an anonymous socket.io-client, capture all 'challenge solved' events for 10 seconds, and assert every payload lacks a `flag` key; with `showSolvedNotifications` disabled assert no event arrives at all.
Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/200.html

threats.title: [F-064] Unbounded regex on socket input (lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts:46)
threats.description:
An attacker opens many anonymous sockets and floods `verifySvgInjectionChallenge` with maximum-size payloads. Each event runs a backtracking regular expression carrying a leading `.*` and a lazy `[\w/-]*?` quantifier over the whole attacker-controlled string, synchronously on the single Node event loop that also serves the REST API on port 3000. Neither a payload size option nor any per-socket or per-connection event rate limit is configured, so the attacker converts cheap event emission into stalled request handling for every other user.

Impact: A single anonymous client can saturate the Node event loop of the process that also serves the REST API on port 3000, degrading or stalling the whole application for all users without authenticating.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-400
CVSS v4: 6.9 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:L/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts:46 evaluates `data?.match(/.*\.\.\/\.\.\/\.\.[\w/-]*?\/redirect\?to=https?:\/\/cataas.com\/cat.*/)` directly on the client-supplied payload with no length check. A grep of both component files for `maxHttpBufferSize`, `rateLimit`, `rate-limit`, and `throttle` returned zero hits, and line 20 shows the Socket.IO server is constructed with `cors` as its only option, so the default message size governs and no event rate limit exists.
- lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts:46

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-064 (F-064)
threats.mitigation:
M-064 — Rate-limit expensive requests and bound input size (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Set an explicit `maxHttpBufferSize` on the Socket.IO server options at lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts:20, sized to the largest legitimate verification payload rather than the default megabyte.
2. Reject oversized or non-string payloads at the top of each `socket.on` handler before any matching runs, and apply a per-socket event rate limit that disconnects a socket exceeding it.
3. Rewrite the regex at line 46 to remove the leading `.*` and the lazy quantifier, anchoring it and matching the path components explicitly so match cost stays linear in input length.
4. Add a load test that emits oversized verifySvgInjectionChallenge payloads at high rate and asserts REST endpoint latency on the same port stays within budget.
Verification: Emit 200 verifySvgInjectionChallenge events of 1 MB each from a script while polling `GET /rest/admin/application-version`; median response latency must stay under 200 ms and oversized payloads must be rejected.
Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/400.html

data.name: Web3 / Wallet / NFT Surface
data.description: Blockchain/web3 endpoints handling wallet addresses, NFT minting, and on-chain key material (ethers). Internet-facing crypto-asset surface with its own key-handling and ownership-verification trust boundary.

threats.title: [F-031] Hardcoded wallet mnemonic in source (routes/checkKeys.ts:10)
threats.description:
An attacker reads the twelve-word BIP-39 mnemonic committed at routes/checkKeys.ts:10, replays HDNodeWallet.fromPhrase locally to derive the same private key the server derives at line 11, and thereby holds the application's blockchain identity without ever touching the running service.

Impact: The application's blockchain identity is fully compromised: an attacker can drain the wallet's balance, transfer or mint NFTs under that identity, and the mnemonic cannot be rotated without a code change and redeployment.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-321
CVSS v4: 8.7 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
routes/checkKeys.ts:10 stores the mnemonic as a source literal and line 11 derives the wallet from it, so the private key at line 12 is reproducible by anyone with read access to the repository.
- routes/checkKeys.ts:10

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-031 (F-031)
threats.mitigation:
M-031 — Move cryptographic keys to a managed secret store (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Load the mnemonic from a required environment variable or secret manager in routes/checkKeys.ts, fail startup when it is absent, generate a fresh mnemonic and migrate any assets off the exposed wallet, and purge the literal from source.
2. Add a startup test asserting the process exits with a configuration error when the mnemonic variable is unset, and a repository check asserting no BIP-39 phrase literal remains under routes/.
Verification: git grep -n 'purpose betray marriage' -- routes/ must return no matches, and starting the server without the mnemonic environment variable must fail with a configuration error rather than boot.
Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/321.html

threats.title: [F-041] Unverified wallet ownership claim (routes/nftMint.ts:41)
threats.description:
An attacker reads any minter address from the public Sepolia NFT contract, then POSTs that address as walletAddress to /rest/web3/walletNFTVerify. The handler takes the wallet identity straight from the request body and looks it up in addressesMinted without ever asking the caller to sign a nonce with the corresponding private key, so the attacker is credited with a mint performed by a wallet it does not control.

Impact: On-chain actions performed by one wallet are attributed to whoever names that address, so the component's ownership-verification boundary conveys no assurance about who controls a wallet.

Risk: Medium (likelihood High, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-290
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
routes/nftMint.ts:41 assigns the wallet identity directly from req.body.walletAddress; a zero-hit search across all four component route files shows no signature-recovery or SIWE verification anywhere in the component.
- routes/nftMint.ts:41

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-1 external → api-server (internet-facing): The boundary assumes every request crossing it carries an authenticated identity, but this handler derives the acting wallet identity from the request body alone.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-041 (F-041)
threats.mitigation:
M-041 — Require a signed nonce challenge before accepting walletAddress in routes/nftMi… (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Issue a server-generated single-use nonce per verification attempt, require the client to return the wallet signature over that nonce, and recover the signer with ethers verifyMessage before comparing it against addressesMinted in routes/nftMint.ts:41.
2. Add an integration test that POSTs a foreign wallet address with no signature to /rest/web3/walletNFTVerify and asserts the response is a rejection rather than success:true.
Verification: curl -s -X POST http://localhost:3000/rest/web3/walletNFTVerify -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"walletAddress":"0x41427790c94E7a592B17ad694eD9c06A02bb9C39"}' must return success:false with a missing-signature error, not a solved challenge.
Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/290.html

threats.title: [F-042] Open redirect via substring allowlist (routes/redirect.ts:19)
threats.description:
An attacker appends an allowlisted URL as a query parameter of its own host, for example /redirect?to=https://evil.example/?r=https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop. security.isRedirectAllowed accepts the value because it tests url.includes(allowedUrl) rather than an exact or origin match, and routes/redirect.ts:19 then issues a 302 to the attacker host from the application's own trusted origin.

Impact: The application lends its own origin to attacker-chosen destinations, enabling credible phishing against shop users and leakage of referrer-borne parameters to a third-party host.

Risk: Medium (likelihood High, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-601
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
routes/redirect.ts:19 calls res.redirect(toUrl) with the raw query value after a guard that lib/insecurity.ts:136 implements as url.includes(allowedUrl), which matches the allowlisted string at any position in the attacker's URL.
- routes/redirect.ts:19

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-042 (F-042)
threats.mitigation:
M-042 — Validate redirect targets against an allowlist (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Parse the submitted value with the WHATWG URL parser and accept it only when the full normalized href equals an entry of security.redirectAllowlist, or when the resolved origin is in an explicit origin allowlist, before routes/redirect.ts:19 executes the redirect.
2. Add a negative test asserting that /redirect?to=https://evil.example/?r=https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop returns 406 instead of a 302 to evil.example.
Verification: curl -sI 'http://localhost:3000/redirect?to=https://evil.example/?r=https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop' must return 406 and no Location header pointing at evil.example.
Reference: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Unvalidated_Redirects_and_Forwards_Cheat_Sheet.html

threats.title: [F-066] Unbounded in-memory set growth (routes/web3Wallet.ts:16)
threats.description:
An attacker sends a stream of unauthenticated POSTs to /rest/web3/walletExploitAddress, each carrying a distinct walletAddress string. routes/web3Wallet.ts:16 adds every value to the process-global walletsConnected set before any validation, and entries are removed only when a matching on-chain ContractExploited event arrives, so the set grows without any cap, eviction, or expiry until the Node process exhausts its heap.

Impact: A single unauthenticated client can drive the API server process to heap exhaustion, taking down the shared Express application rather than just the web3 endpoints.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-400
CVSS v4: 6.9 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:L/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
routes/web3Wallet.ts:16 executes walletsConnected.add(metamaskAddress) on the request path with no size limit, TTL, or address-format check, and a zero-hit search for rate limiting across the component route files shows no request-rate bound on the endpoint.
- routes/web3Wallet.ts:16

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-066 (F-066)
threats.mitigation:
M-066 — Rate-limit expensive requests and bound input size (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Validate the submitted value as an Ethereum address before routes/web3Wallet.ts:16 stores it, replace the unbounded Set with a size-capped TTL cache, and register the express-rate-limit middleware already used at server.ts:343 on the /rest/web3 routes.
2. Add a load test that posts 50000 distinct addresses and asserts both that the retained entry count stays at the configured cap and that excess requests are rejected with 429.
Verification: Send 50000 distinct walletAddress values to /rest/web3/walletExploitAddress and confirm the process resident heap stays flat and that requests beyond the configured rate return HTTP 429.
Reference: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Denial_of_Service_Cheat_Sheet.html
